To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) RNN language models trained on large amounts of text data exhibit preferences for certain syntactic alternations, and these preferences are similar to those shown by humans in acceptability judgment experiments, and (2) RNN language model surprisals correlate well with human surprisals, and are better predictors of human surprisals than an n-gram model.
RNN language model representations of syntax exhibit a preference for word orders that humans find more acceptable, and that this is not the case for a simple n-gram language model baseline.
RNNs trained to predict the next word in a sentence learn the abstract word order preferences of humans in syntactic alternation tasks.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how much RNNs learn about syntax, and we take a novel approach to answering it.
how RNNs learn syntactic knowledge.
whether RNNs can learn abstract word order constraints.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
RNNs are not capable of learning the human-like abstract word-order preferences.
RNNs do learn abstract word order features and preferences.
RNN language model surprisals are similar to human acceptability ratings in a range of alternations, and this similarity is not due to the RNNs learning simple cooccurrence statistics.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the recurrent neural network (RNN) is able to capture the abstract word order preferences in the language.
RNNs can learn humanlike abstract word order preferences.
RNN language model learn human-like syntactic preferences.
The main takeaway from our work is that
RNNs do learn human-like preferences in a range of syntactic alternation tasks, and that the RNN models’ performance in these tasks is similar to human acceptability ratings.
RNNs do seem to learn abstract word order constraints, but they learn them in an incomplete and noisy way.
RNNs trained for language modeling learn abstract features which underlie human-like syntactic alternation preferences.
